title: Dance halls and pavilions in Mandeville, Covington, Bogalusa and Abita Springs
summary: Where dances were held across the lake, and a digression on Abita Springs water and the restful pine country.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: What did Buddy play in Mandeville? Would he play in a dance hall or in a pavilion?
No, he played in a pavilion, in most cases, called Jackson Park, which was on the outskirts of Mandeville.
Is that right on the lake? Right off the lake, yes. I think that's still standing, is it?

It may, possibly it is still there. In Covington, as an example, they would play at, well, there was a St. Tammany Fairgrounds, and of course, each year at the fair there would be dancing and orchestras. Then there was Vogue Folia Park, which is right near the center of Covington. Then there were also dances at the old Southern Hotel in Covington. In Bogalusa, I can't remember, I think the name of the place that the dances were given was the Pine Tree Inn, but I'm not sure about that. And in Abita Springs, it was the town pavilion, and it was right close to the famous real Abita Springs. In other words, the dance hall was right above the springs. You could walk down from the dance hall to the springs.
And what's famous about those springs, anyway?
Well, it's supposed to be the purest water in this part of the country, very healthful. People would go there to drink this water, and it was quite a health resort back in those days.
That's very restful over there. That's funny that you go there and you relax and everything. I don't know why it is.
Well, it's very restful country, pine country over there.
See, I asked you about Leonard Parker and Dan Moody. You don't remember them?
I don't remember them. No, I don't.
Black Eagle Vels there. You don't remember them? Those are people George Lewis has mentioned to me, playing over there. Who are some of the people you heard here in town?
